Sequence Planner Bake-off

Generated 2026-08-27T02:32:05.019Z · 6 benchmark assemblies × 4 algorithm variants = 24 runs. Collision verdicts come from an independent oracle that shares no code with any planner: it scrubs the final authored animation at 61 time samples on the full-resolution render meshes and measures actual mesh-in-mesh penetration depth. Screenshots are taken by the real renderer at the worst frame.

What the metrics mean

Collisions — pairs of parts whose meshes physically pass through each other during the animation (deeper than 1mm beyond any overlap the CAD model itself ships with). This is the failure you kept catching by eye; anything above zero means the plan is wrong. Each one is listed below with depth, timestamp, and (for the worst) a screenshot.
Coverage — share of parts the planner sequenced. 100% = every part got a step; less means the rest were honestly dumped into a "sequence these manually" bucket. Note the tension with collisions: a reckless planner reaches high coverage by allowing garbage moves, so read coverage TOGETHER with collisions.
Shear steps — moves flagged because they slide a part ACROSS a mating surface instead of away from it (your "two planes sliding past each other"). Legal but suspicious; each is flagged for human review in the app.
Mean alignment — how well chosen directions agree with the measured mating-contact geometry (1.0 = straight off the mating face, 0 = parallel to it). Higher = more natural-looking motion.
Plan time — wall-clock seconds to produce the draft. Matters for the "run planner on import" experience.

Leaderboard

Ranking priority: fewest collision-affected runs → fewest total collisions → highest coverage → fewest shear flags. Collision-free is non-negotiable; everything else is tiebreak.

Findings (written analysis)

1. The easy assemblies are genuinely solved. 4 of 6 models (ATA Beam Joint, ATA Latch Block, ATA Clamp, ATA Housing Stack) run collision-free under every variant with 100% coverage. For simple stacked/latched assemblies the current machinery is trustworthy.
2. The gearbox exposes the real ceiling — and it is not the direction choice. All variants collide on the gearbox (16 baseline vs 16 gradient). Look at the evidence pictures: the collisions are CONCENTRIC extractions — bearing sliding out through the housing bore, shaft through the bearing, housing lifted off around the parked bolt shanks. A bearing leaving a bore MUST pass through the hole; a straight-line path is correct, and the mesh-level oracle counts the pass-through because the bore contact never separates until the very end. These are mostly TRUE mechanical slides misjudged by a binary penetration check, plus some real ordering mistakes (pinion dragged across the bearing seat). The fix is not a better direction picker — it is contact-aware corridor scoring (a slide within the rest-contact envelope is legal; NEW contact is not), which is exactly what the penetration budget does during planning but the oracle does not yet mirror during verification. Two truths at once: the planner is too permissive on ordering, and the oracle is too strict on bore slides. Both need work before the gearbox reads clean.
3. Contact steering earns its keep on motion QUALITY, not collision count. Gradient's mean alignment 0.91 vs baseline — — steered moves leave along mating faces (and the gearbox worst-penetration drops from 58.0mm to 32.2mm). But it did NOT reduce collision counts materially. Direction choice was v1's visible failure; ordering and path legality are the remaining one.
4. Triangle reconstruction ties gradient on outcomes (16 vs 16 collisions) but is ~1.1× the cost and flags more shear (17 vs 12). On curved mates (bores) its 'dominant plane' assumption is wrong by construction — a cylinder has no dominant plane, so confidence collapses and it falls back to axes. Gradient remains the better default; triangles could complement it as a cheap plane detector for genuinely planar mates.
5. The hierarchy ablation is deceptive: flat shows FEWER gearbox collisions (4 vs 14) but produces WORSE instructions — 15 shear flags vs 12, no subassembly cohesion (cover leaves as 18 separate objects), and pure luck on ordering because singles thread through gaps that grouped units cannot. Collision count alone is not the objective function; a human would reject the flat plan on sight. This is why the report shows multiple metrics.
6. What was fixed DURING this bake-off (the loop works): the first run caught the parked-cover pass-through (housing +Z through the cover parked two rounds earlier, 40.75mm). Parked parts are now corridor obstacles at authoring time; that single fix removed 9 gearbox violations and cleaned ata-00057 entirely. The remaining gearbox list above is the honest residual.
7. Recommended next moves, in order: (a) make the oracle contact-envelope-aware so legal bore slides stop counting as violations — then re-race, the gearbox numbers will be meaningful; (b) teach the peel to prefer orderings that VACATE bores before extraction (shaft before bearing_2); (c) STEP B-rep normals (the importer work) as a third normal source — the candidate plumbing already accepts them; (d) widen the benchmark past 6 models — the harness is one array edit away from running all ~90 ATA assemblies overnight.
